0044.event: The Lake Walkers takes its name from fossils found near ancient lake shores in Kenya, dating to about four million two hundred thousand years ago. The bones belong to very early members of the human family, creatures who still climbed with long arms yet walked upright on two legs. Their remains settled into lake mud and silt, where hippos and crocodiles also lived, and were preserved as the lake beds hardened into stone. Scientists read these fossils as a bridge between tree dwelling apes and ground walking humans. They did not know they were becoming us. They only knew the shore, the water, and the slow work of survival, one upright step at a time.
0044.announce: Here is a poem about the first walkers at the lakeshore: The Lake Walkers.
0044.title: The Lake Walkers
0044.piece:
I came down to the water where the tall reeds grew,
and heard soft splashing long before they came in view.
Half upright through the papyrus, through the sedge they went,
with arms that still remembered what the branches meant.
Climbing arms and walking legs, one body torn between
the trees it used to live in and the ground as yet unseen.
They waded where the hippos rolled, they drank, they fed, they played,
and left their bones in Kenyan mud, where time and silt have stayed.
They did not know the future. They only knew the shore.
But they were us already, walking, wanting more.

0045.event: A Jaw in the Mud tells of a fossil jawbone found in Kenya, laid down about four million one hundred fifty thousand years ago. The teeth are small, flat, and worn the way human teeth wear, but the skull they belonged to was built like an ape's, with a small brain. No tools lay beside it. No fire had been tamed. There were no words to mark the day it died. Yet this mouth bit and chewed, and the feet below it walked upright on the open ground. The jaw sits at the very edge of our family story, where the ape ends and the human begins, or rather where the two are still the same creature. It is a reminder that we did not arrive all at once. First came the teeth, and the walking feet.
0045.announce: A story of the oldest mouth that walked upright: A Jaw in the Mud.
0045.title: A Jaw in the Mud
0045.piece:
The trench was peeled back layer by layer, and there it lay: a jawbone older than any name. The teeth were almost human, flat and worn and small. The skull it belonged to was ape, all ape, of the old world still.
Between those two truths, a creature had learned to stand up. No tools. No fire. No words. Just a mouth that bit, and feet that walked away.
Hold it in your mind. This is the oldest bargain our family ever made. Give up the trees, keep the teeth, and walk.

0046.event: The Middle Awash Striders takes its name from fossil leg bones found in Ethiopia, about four million one hundred thousand years old. Shin and thigh lie in order, and they tell a plain story: the walk had already won. The stride is upright, heel down and toe off, the same rhythm every human uses today. Yet the fingers of these same creatures still hooked like a climber's, ready for the branch. Above the waist, the old ape. Below it, the new human. The fossils come from the Middle Awash valley, a place that has kept more of our early story than anywhere else on earth. They show that walking did not arrive all at once. It won the legs first, and let the hands keep the trees a while longer.
0046.announce: For the stride that won, a marching verse: The Middle Awash Striders.
0046.title: The Middle Awash Striders
0046.piece:
Heel, arch, push. Heel, arch, push.
The same beat marches on, from then to us.
The fingers hooked the branch above,
but the feet had found the ground they love.
Heel down first, then the weight rolls through,
the push, the swing, the stride made new.
An ape's arms and a human's feet,
the ancient and the new complete.
The walking won without a sound.
It simply claimed the open ground.

0047.event: Night Nests is about how the early walkers slept. By day they moved on two legs across the open ground, but when the sun went down they climbed back into the trees. There, like the great apes of today, they wove sleeping nests from branches, small warm platforms high above the reach of leopards. The fingers that still hooked branches were good for this work. Below, in the dark, the hunters moved. Above, curled out of sight, the walkers breathed slow and slept. They were half out of the trees now, but not all the way. The ground was for the day. The trees were still for the night. It would be a long time before any of our family dared sleep on the ground.
0047.announce: A soft song for the sleepers in the trees: Night Nests.
0047.title: Night Nests
0047.piece:
Climb up, climb up, when the sun goes down,
weave the branches round and round.
Leopard prowls on the ground below,
but the nest is high where the cool winds blow.
Sleep, small walkers, soft and deep,
the trees will keep you while you sleep.
Day is for walking, far and wide.
Night is for the nest, where you hide.
Morning will come with the sun's first call.
Climb down, climb down, walkers all.

0048.event: The First Long Journeys tells of foot bones built for distance. Short toes, strong arches, legs made to keep going: these are the feet of creatures that walked the savanna for hours at a time. They moved from water hole to water hole under a hard sun, learning the seasons the way all travelers must. They learned where the grass goes brown and where the tubers hide. No beast walks that far without a reason, and no feet are shaped that way by accident. Distance was their first invention. Before tools, before fire, before words, they learned to walk far and walk well. The line of backs moving across the afternoon shimmer, two legs and one rhythm, was the beginning of every journey our family would ever take.
0048.announce: A song of the long trail: The First Long Journeys.
0048.title: The First Long Journeys
0048.piece:
Three hours walking neath the sky like coal,
then gold at evening, water hole to hole.
Short toes, strong arches, built for the trail,
they learned the seasons without fail.
Where grass goes brown and tubers hide,
they walked the savanna far and wide.
Two legs, one rhythm, steady and true.
They walked the morning, and the whole day through.
Distance was the first thing they made true.
The rest came later. First, they walked it through.

0049.event: The Passing of the Torch marks a changing of the guard among the early walkers. About three million nine hundred thousand years ago, one kind of upright ape was fading from the fossil record of East Africa. In its place, a cousin was spreading: Australopithecus afarensis, with a longer, freer stride, moving across the region in growing numbers. The old bones are the final pages of one story. The new bones are the first pages of another. This is how evolution works, not with trumpets but with quiet replacement. The torch does not burn. It walks. It passes from one hand to another, and it does not return to the hand that held it. Someone younger always picks it up and runs.
0049.announce: A poem for the changing of the guard: The Passing of the Torch.
0049.title: The Passing of the Torch
0049.piece:
One kind of walker fades among the thorn,
and one comes on, like night gives way to morn.
The old bones close their story in the dust.
The new bones stride. The change is slow, but just.
No trumpet sounds. No banner is unfurled.
The torch walks on around the world.
It does not burn. It passes hand to hand.
You carry it a while across the land,
then set it down. The young ones pick it up
and run. That is the road. That is the cup
we all must drink: to walk, to pass, to go,
and trust the young to carry what we know.

0050.event: The Plain of Ash tells of the day a volcano dusted the Laetoli plain in Tanzania with fine grey ash. The mountain cleared its throat, and the sky went grey, and the ash fell soft as snow across the grass. No one alive saw it happen, but the earth remembers. That thin white layer would soon keep a record no hand ever wrote: footprints, pressed in a single morning, hardened to stone. For now, the plain was only white and waiting. The wind did not know what was coming. The ash did not know what it would hold. But the ground was getting ready to remember, and remember it would, for three million eight hundred thousand years.
0050.announce: A short verse on the day the sky turned grey: The Plain of Ash.
0050.title: The Plain of Ash
0050.piece:
The mountain cleared its throat.
The sky went grey.
The plain of Laetoli
went white that day.
Fine ash, soft ash,
laid down like snow.
The ground got ready.
The wind didn't know.
Something was coming.
The ash would keep
what the morning gave it,
fast asleep.
White page, white morning,
no hand, no pen.
The earth was waiting
to remember then.

0051.event: A Mother's Arms is about a female whose arm bones were long and strong. She did not use that strength for climbing or fighting. She used it for carrying. A child, a year, two years, three years more, riding her hip while she walked the open ground, one arm around the small warm weight. The plains were wide and full of teeth, and she carried and she walked, and the two breaths kept time together. That is how we got here. Not by the strongest arm or the sharpest stone, but by someone who never stopped carrying. Long before words, before tools, before fire, there was this: a mother who would not put the child down.
0051.announce: A letter to the first mother: A Mother's Arms.
0051.title: A Mother's Arms
0051.piece:
To the one who carried:
I held your arm bones in my hands and knew at once what the strength was for. Not the branch. Not the fight. The child. A year, two years, three, riding your hip across the open ground while the teeth prowled far off. One arm around the small warm weight. Two breaths, keeping time.
You never put the child down, and so we are here. Everything else came later: the stone, the fire, the word. First came you, walking, carrying. Sleep now. We remember.

0052.event: The Crossing at Laetoli is the most famous walk ever taken. About three million seven hundred thousand years ago, fresh volcanic ash covered a plain in Tanzania. By mid morning, at least three of our ancient cousins crossed it, walking side by side. The first walked tall. The second stepped inside the first one's prints. Small behind them came a third, a child, learning the same heel and toe rhythm. Then the rain came, soft, stippling the ash, and hardened it to stone. The prints kept everything: the deep heel, the rising arch, the push of the toes. A family going somewhere, single file and wide. Not by a hand, not by a plan, just feet that walked because the walking felt complete. The first road ever made.
0052.announce: A poem of three walkers in fresh ash: The Crossing at Laetoli.
0052.title: The Crossing at Laetoli
0052.piece:
Fresh ash at dawn. By mid morning, three
walkers crossed the whiteness, wild and free:
the tall one first, the second in their track,
the little one behind, no looking back.
Heel, arch, toe. The mud took every press.
Then rain came soft and stippled every line,
and turned the morning into stone, and time
has kept it. Three million years, and still they go:
heel, arch, toe, through ash and rain and snow
of ages. No hand made this road, no plan.
Just feet that walked. Walk on, as we began.

0053.event: The Smallest Footprints belongs to the child at Laetoli. Among the famous trails, the tiniest prints step carefully inside the largest ones. The little one was tired, perhaps, or simply wise: it chose the deep print of the adult, where each step was already made, where the walking was cheap. The plain was wide and the morning wild, but safe inside those larger, older steps, the child walked on. That is how the smallest of us grows: inside the steps of someone who went first, thirst quenched by someone else's effort. Every child steps in footprints not their own. Three million seven hundred thousand years ago, one already did.
0053.announce: A small verse for the smallest feet: The Smallest Footprints.
0053.title: The Smallest Footprints
0053.piece:
Small feet, big prints.
The child was wise:
step where the steps
are already sized.
The plain was wide,
the morning new.
The big ones led.
The small walked through.
Inside their toes,
the young one grew.
That's how we learn:
we follow through.

0054.event: Rain on the Trail is about what fell after the walkers passed. The clouds came low, and rain dropped onto the fresh ash, each drop pocking the footprints' rims with tiny craters. That stippled skin is proof of timing: the prints were only hours old when the storm began. One morning's journey, that is the whole of it. Three walkers, rain, and a patch of ground that kept their going. The weather signed the page. The ash said they were here. The rain said this age, this hour, this morning. Without that rain, the trail might have blown away, and we would never have known. With it, the stone remembers a single day three million six hundred eighty thousand years ago.
0054.announce: A poem about the rain that signed its name: Rain on the Trail.
0054.title: Rain on the Trail
0054.piece:
After they passed, the clouds came low and broke,
and rain fell on the ash, each drop a stroke
that pocked the rims, a stippled skin of stone.
The prints were hours old. The storm had shown
its water praise. One morning, that was all:
three walkers, rain, the ash, the squall.
The weather signed the page. The stone agreed
to keep it. Three million years of seed
and season since, and still the trail is clear:
they walked this morning. They were here.

0443.event: The Village Age Ends marks the rise of the first cities, around five thousand years ago. From the Nile valley to the plains between the Tigris and Euphrates, from the Indus valley to the Yellow River, farming villages grew into walled towns and then into cities. With cities came kings, priests, scribes, markets, and armies. Writing was invented to count grain and goods. Laws were carved to govern crowds. The old life of small villages, where everyone knew everyone, gave way to streets, temples, and palaces. Civilization, with all its wonders and all its cruelties, had begun, and the human story would never be small again.
0443.announce: The following poem walks from the first planted seed to the first city wall: The Village Age Ends.
0443.title: The Village Age Ends
0443.piece:
From the Nile to the Yangtze, cities rose where villages stood,
and the first long chapter of the human story closed for good.
I stood upon a hill and looked across ten thousand years:
the first wild harvest, the first sown seed,
the first shaped pot, the first warm loaf, the first tame herd,
all of it leading here, to walls and crowded streets,
to kings and scribes and markets, to the humming of the town.
The wanderers had put down roots. The roots became fields.
The fields became cities. And I had walked each step beside them.
The village age was over. The story was just beginning.
